newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich sees conservative support for budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich sees conservative support for budget deal.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich predicted Saturday that the new balanced-budget deal would garner support from conservatives in Congress, saying he hoped to see entitlement reform and tax reduction bills signed into law by July 4.
Speaking to reporters in his home district, the Georgia Republican said the White House helped set the stage for Friday's landmark agreement by adopting a more "moderate" negotiating posture.
"It's a remarkably conservative budget agreement to have with a liberal Democrat in the White House," the Georgia Republican said.

The agreement faces months of negotiations as Congress tries to iron out details of $85 billion in anticipated tax cuts, $34 billion in new spending for President Clinton and $115 billion in savings to assure the solvency of the Medicare medical insurance plan for the poor and elderly.
The deal has been criticised by some conservatives who say tax cuts are not deep enough.
But Gingrich said that over a 10-year period, the budget plan could save $600-$700 billion from entitlement programmes while making room for $250 billion in tax cuts and higher defence spending.
"From every reasonable standpoint, this is a budget that every conservative ought to vote for," he said.

The speaker also claimed the budget agreement as a victory for his party's Contract With America, the 1994 manifesto that first helped Republicans take control of Congress by laying out a new conservative legislative agenda.

Bolstered by the 1994 election results, Gingrich led Republicans into a stormy budget standoff with the White House which shut the federal government down twice and sent his own popularity ratings plummeting.

"It took us four years and two elections," Gingrich said Saturday. "The re-election of the Republican Congress in November was a signal that the country really wanted to get a balanced budget and lower taxes."

Gingrich said budget negotiators were able to reach agreement this time because White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles was less inclined to defend cuts in federal programmes than his predecessor, Leon Panetta.
"I think the appointment of Erskine Bowles was a sign that they wanted a common-sense Southern moderate businessman rather than one of the people who'd created the modern welfare programme," he said.
Gingrich said he wanted to see balanced-budget legislation passed by Congress and signed into law by President Clinton before this year's July 4 Independence Day holiday.
"The details are going to take a long time to work out," he later said in a speech to Republican women.
"But I would like to see the bills passed and signed into law by July 4. I think that would be a great birthday gift to the United States."
